title: Coordinates to Address: Reverse Geocode Lookup
description: Turn latitude and longitude into a structured address with Coordinates to Address — the reverse of geocoding, done openly. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, 38.8977, -77.0365 — the White House's coordinates — reverse-geocode to 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue NW, Washington, DC, in structured parts.
quick_answer: Coordinates to Address reverse-geocodes a latitude and longitude pair into a structured address — street, town, region and country as separate fields. Paste the coordinates and read the address, ready for records, reports and any form that thinks in streets rather than degrees.
steps_intro: Coordinates are exact and unreadable; addresses are the opposite. Convert to the human format:

A pin dropped in the wrong field reverse-geocodes to a road that is not yours — the cheapest error check in mapping.
Systems that captured a location as numbers eventually must tell a human where it was. Structured fields beat a raw pair in every filing cabinet.
The day's surveyed points become the day's named places — the report writes itself once the names exist.
38.8977, -77.0365 resolves to the White House's address — a useful sanity anchor: if a reverse geocoder cannot name that lawn, distrust it everywhere.

body.t: A point in open country returns the nearest named road and town, labelled by its own coarseness. A sparse answer is the truth at that precision, not a failure.

faq: Is this the same as a reverse geocoder?
Yes — 'reverse geocoding' is the technical name for coordinates → address, and this page is exactly that, presented in structured fields.
Can I use the tool without sharing my precise location?
Yes — you paste the coordinates under study. Your own position is not requested.
Why might a boundary or place name look different elsewhere?
Different geocoders hold different data vintages and naming choices — contested names most visibly. The fields show this source's answer.
Does MapBench store my browser location?
No.
What coordinate formats are accepted?
Decimal degrees (38.8977, -77.0365) is the native tongue. Order is latitude first — swapped pairs are the most common error in the field.
The address came back as just a town.
Then the point sits where the map knows the town but not the street — common in rural areas. The coarse answer is the honest resolution at that data depth.
Forward instead — address to coordinates?
The Address to Coordinates tool runs this backwards.
Coordinates from a photo's EXIF?
Paste them — naming where a photo was taken is this tool's daily bread, provided the photo kept its location data.
The road name looks outdated.
Maps rename slowly and geocoders lag politely. The structured fields show the source's current word; local signage is newer still.
Can it name a place at sea?
Coastal points may return the nearest shore address or nothing structured — the honest output for a point with no street.
